size.note: Newman's Birds gives 11–12 cm, and 34 cm for the breeding bird.

habitat: Usually one male with several females, in a wide variety of habitats including suburbia. It parasitises the Common Waxbill.
summary: A common resident. The breeding male is a small pied bird with a red bill and a very long tail. The red bill is kept in non-breeding plumage. The female has a pinkish-brown bill and bolder head stripes than the female Shaft-tailed Whydah. The courting male hovers and calls 'peetzy-peetzy-peetzy'. In normal flight it calls 'tseet-tseet-tseet'. The Kemp name Pintailed Whydah and the code RB were left unchanged.

similar.note: Shaft-tailed Whydah has buff underparts and thin tail shafts with broadened ends. Its female has less distinctive head markings.

head.pattern: The red bill is kept in non-breeding plumage.
Pinkish-brown. Bolder head stripes than the female Shaft-tailed Whydah.

viewNotes.note: Small and pied, with a red bill and a very long tail.
The courting male hovers, describing a circle in the vertical plane.
Pinkish-brown bill and bold head stripes.
The underside in flight is not described.

calls.description: A continuous wispy 'peetzy-peetzy-peetzy' while hovering, and 'tseet-tseet-tseet' in normal flight. The grade A call is from Shaw Park in the Eastern Cape. The filename is XC353667-Pin-tailed Whydah xc.mp3.

research.note: Newman calls it a common resident, and Avibase does not mark it rare, so all twelve months are listed. The stored length covers 11–12 cm and the 34 cm breeding length. The grade A call is from the Eastern Cape. The Kemp name Pintailed Whydah and the code RB were left unchanged.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^15=32768 mature individuals (resident breeder); paper interval half–double → 16384–65536.
